lead: A real band-pass signal carries its information in a narrow band around a carrier, so the carrier itself is only a vehicle. The Hilbert transform gives a 90° shifted copy of the signal; adding it as an imaginary part makes the analytic signal, which has only positive frequencies. Removing the carrier from the analytic signal leaves the complex envelope, a low-pass signal whose real and imaginary parts are the in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components. SSB transmitters, I/Q modulators, digital receivers and simulators all use this idea.
prereq: You need: Fourier transform review and band-pass signals, in particular the canonical form xI cos − xQ sin.

blocks.text: A real signal has a conjugate-symmetric spectrum, X(−f) = X*(f): the negative-frequency half is the mirror image of the positive half and carries nothing new. The Hilbert transform produces a companion signal x̂(t) whose every frequency component is shifted by 90° while its magnitude stays the same.

blocks.where: the integral runs over all τ and is taken as a Cauchy principal value, which steps symmetrically round the point τ = t; x̂(t) is in volts. In words, x̂(t) = x(t) * 1/(πt).
sgn(f) = 1 for f > 0, −1 for f < 0 and 0 at f = 0. So H(f) = −j (a −90° shift) for positive frequencies and +j (a +90° shift) for negative frequencies.

items: Cosine becomes sine: the Hilbert transform of cos(2πf<sub>0</sub>t + θ) is sin(2πf<sub>0</sub>t + θ), for f<sub>0</sub> > 0.
Sine becomes minus cosine: the transform of sin(2πf<sub>0</sub>t + θ) is −cos(2πf<sub>0</sub>t + θ).
A constant (f = 0) has transform zero, and applying the transform twice gives −x(t).
x(t) and x̂(t) have the same energy (or power) and are orthogonal: ∫ x(t) x̂(t) dt = 0.
For a message m(t) band-limited below f<sub>c</sub>, the transform of m(t) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) is m(t) sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t): only the carrier is shifted.
The ideal transformer is non-causal; a practical 90° phase-shift network or digital filter approximates it over the band of interest.

blocks.text: The analytic signal, also called the pre-envelope, is xa(t) = x(t) + j x̂(t). Its spectrum is X(f) + j(−j sgn f)X(f) = [1 + sgn(f)]X(f): 2X(f) for f > 0 and 0 for f < 0. The negative frequencies cancel and the positive ones double, so Re{xa(t)} is still x(t).

The complex envelope removes the carrier: x̃(t) = xa(t) e−j2πfct. In frequency, X̃(f) = Xa(f + fc): the doubled positive band slides down to sit around 0 Hz. It is low-pass and complex, and it is not the analytic signal, which still contains ej2πfct.

Writing x̃(t) = xI(t) + j xQ(t) gives the canonical representation, x(t) = Re{x̃(t) ej2πfct} = xI(t) cos(2πfct) − xQ(t) sin(2πfct). In polar form, the natural envelope is a(t) = |x̃(t)| = |xa(t)| = √(xI² + xQ²) and the phase is φ(t) = tan−1(xQ/xI), so x(t) = a(t) cos(2πfct + φ(t)).

A receiver finds I and Q by downconversion: multiply x(t) by 2cos(2πfct) and by −2sin(2πfct), then low-pass filter each product. For the first, 2x cos = xI(1 + cos 4πfct) − xQ sin 4πfct, and the filter keeps xI. Upconversion runs the other way: the transmitter forms xI cos − xQ sin.

sections.h3: Low-pass equivalent of a band-pass system

blocks.text: A band-pass filter with real impulse response h(t) also has a complex envelope h̃(t), defined by h(t) = Re{h̃(t) e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>}. With that definition the output complex envelope is ỹ(t) = ½ x̃(t) * h̃(t), and the real output is y(t) = Re{ỹ(t) e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>}. The ½ comes from writing both signals with the same Re{·} rule; some books define h̃ with a factor 2 and then drop the ½. Keep one convention: mixing them changes the gain by a factor 2, which is 6 dB.

Some syllabi call the complex envelope the low-pass equivalent. It turns band-pass filtering, modulation and noise into low-pass problems with complex numbers, and a simulator can run at a sample rate set by the bandwidth instead of by the carrier. In single-sideband generation one path carries m(t) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) and the other the Hilbert-transformed m̂(t) sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t); subtracting or adding them cancels one sideband (the phase-shift method of SSB modulation).

examples.question: A band-pass voltage is x(t) = 2 cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) V with f<sub>c</sub> > 0. Find x̂(t), the analytic signal x<sub>a</sub>(t), the complex envelope x̃(t), and the I and Q components.
steps: The Hilbert transform of a cosine is the sine with the same phase: x̂(t) = 2 sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) V.
x<sub>a</sub>(t) = x + j x̂ = 2[cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) + j sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°)] = 2e<sup>j(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°)</sup> V.
Remove the carrier: x̃(t) = x<sub>a</sub>(t) e<sup>−j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup> = 2e<sup>j30°</sup> V, a constant for this pure tone.
Rectangular form: 2 cos 30° = 1.732 V and 2 sin 30° = 1.000 V, so x̃ = 1.732 + j1.000 V: I = 1.732 V, Q = 1.000 V.

Check: 1.732 cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − 1.000 sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) = 2[cos 30° cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − sin 30° sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t)] = 2 cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) V. The envelope is |x̃| = √(1.732² + 1²) = 2 V.
examples.answer: x̂ = 2 sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) V; x<sub>a</sub> = 2e<sup>j(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°)</sup> V; x̃ = 1.732 + j1.000 V; I = 1.732 V, Q = 1.000 V; envelope 2 V.

examples.question: A tone x(t) = 2 cos(2π × 1.001 MHz × t) V is described about the reference carrier f<sub>c</sub> = 1 MHz. Find x̃(t), and the I and Q values at t = 0 and t = 0.125 ms.
steps: Write the tone as 2 cos(2π(f<sub>c</sub> + Δ)t) with offset Δ = 1.001 MHz − 1 MHz = 1 kHz.
Analytic signal: x<sub>a</sub>(t) = 2e<sup>j2π(f<sub>c</sub> + Δ)t</sup>. Complex envelope: x̃(t) = 2e<sup>j2πΔt</sup> = 2cos(2π×10³t) + j2sin(2π×10³t) V.
So x<sub>I</sub>(t) = 2cos(2π×10³t) and x<sub>Q</sub>(t) = 2sin(2π×10³t): the complex envelope turns round a circle of radius 2 V once per millisecond.
At t = 0.125 ms the angle is 2π × 10³ × 0.125×10<sup>−3</sup> = π/4 = 45°, so I = 2 cos 45° = 1.414 V and Q = 2 sin 45° = 1.414 V. The envelope stays |x̃| = 2 V.
examples.answer: x̃(t) = 2e<sup>j2π(1000)t</sup> V; at t = 0, (I, Q) = (2, 0) V; at t = 0.125 ms, (I, Q) = (1.414, 1.414) V. A frequency offset makes the complex envelope rotate at the offset frequency.

traps: The Hilbert transform of cos is sin, not −sin. The −j factor delays the positive-frequency phasor by 90°, and cos(θ − 90°) = sin θ.
x̃(t) is not the analytic signal x<sub>a</sub>(t). The analytic signal still contains e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>; the complex envelope has the carrier removed.
H(f) = −j sgn(f), not −j for every frequency. Negative frequencies get +90°, which keeps x̂(t) real.
The complex envelope depends on the reference f<sub>c</sub> you choose. The same tone has a constant x̃ about its own frequency and a rotating x̃ about any other.
In low-pass equivalents keep one convention for the ½. Dropping it, or applying it twice, changes the gain by 6 dB.

quiz.q: State the frequency response of the ideal Hilbert transformer and its phase shift.
quiz.a: H(f) = −j sgn(f). Its magnitude is 1 (0 at f = 0); the phase is −90° for f > 0 and +90° for f < 0.

quiz.q: Why does x<sub>a</sub>(t) = x(t) + j x̂(t) contain no negative frequencies?
quiz.a: Its spectrum is X(f) + j(−j sgn f)X(f) = [1 + sgn(f)]X(f). For f > 0, 1 + sgn f = 2, so the spectrum is 2X(f). For f < 0, 1 + sgn f = 0, so the negative half cancels exactly.

quiz.q: For x(t) = 4 cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t − 45°) V, find x̂(t), x<sub>a</sub>(t), x̃(t), I and Q.
quiz.a: x̂ = 4 sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t − 45°) V; x<sub>a</sub> = 4e<sup>j(2πf<sub>c</sub>t − 45°)</sup> V; x̃ = 4e<sup>−j45°</sup> = 2.828 − j2.828 V; I = 2.828 V, Q = −2.828 V.

quiz.q: A student writes that the Hilbert transform of cos is −sin because −j is a −90° shift. Find the error.
quiz.a: A −90° shift of cos θ gives cos(θ − 90°), which is +sin θ. The student turned the phasor the wrong way. So the transform of cos is sin; it is the transform of sin that is −cos.

quiz.q: Find the complex envelope and the envelope of x(t) = [1 + 0.5 cos(2π×10³t)] cos(2π×10⁶t) V about f<sub>c</sub> = 1 MHz.
quiz.a: The message is band-limited far below f<sub>c</sub>, so x̂ = [1 + 0.5 cos(2π×10³t)] sin(2π×10⁶t). Then x̃ = 1 + 0.5 cos(2π×10³t), real: x<sub>I</sub> = 1 + 0.5 cos(2π×10³t), x<sub>Q</sub> = 0. The envelope swings between 1.5 V and 0.5 V.

quiz.q: Why can a band-pass filter be replaced by a low-pass filter acting on complex envelopes? Mention the factor.
quiz.a: With x = Re{x̃ e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>}, for f > 0 X(f) = ½X̃(f − f<sub>c</sub>), and likewise H(f) = ½H̃(f − f<sub>c</sub>). The output Y = XH near +f<sub>c</sub> is ¼X̃H̃, and Y(f) = ½Ỹ(f − f<sub>c</sub>) there, so Ỹ = ½X̃H̃, that is ỹ = ½ x̃ * h̃: a low-pass operation. The ½ comes from the Re{·} definition used for h̃.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software-defined radios digitise I and Q directly after a quadrature downconverter, so later filtering and demodulation run at a low rate. I/Q gain and phase imbalance and image rejection are practical problems in that chain. Simulation tools use the same complex-envelope view to model a band-pass system as a low-pass one. Search for analytic signal, IQ data and quadrature downconversion.
